quote: "But it is in thy power continuously to fan these thoughts into a flame." — Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book 7.2
context:
This line answers a worry Marcus raises in the same passage: that his principles might simply die on him. His reply is that a principle does not perish on its own. It goes out only when the thoughts that feed it are left to go cold. The image he reaches for is not construction but combustion: a flame that survives not because it is finished, but because someone keeps tending it. The work is never done once. It is done again each day, or it fades.

This week, a downtown St. Louis hotel built in 1913 reopened after standing shuttered for more than two years. 
Le Méridien St. Louis Downtown closed in January 2024 after water damage from a burst sprinkler pipe, and the 96-room hotel, near Pine and Tucker, reopened this week after being closed for more than two years.
 The building never stopped being what it was. It waited for hands to return to it. Most things we value are like this: a craft, a friendship, an attention. They do not require a single great effort but a repeated small one. What goes untended does not break dramatically. It simply cools.
question: What in your life is still standing but gone cold, waiting only for you to return to it?
